To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
mouse cochlear hair cells exhibit a variety of electrical responses in vitro similar to those exhibited in vivo by hair cells in the cochleas and vestibular organs of other mammals.
the hair cells in the organ of Corti of the mouse retain their morphology for at least 5 days in vitro and that they behave electrophysiologically in a similar fashion to their in vivo counterparts.
the hair cells of the mouse cochlear organotypic culture are morphologically and physiologically similar to the hair cells of guinea-pigs in vivo, although there are some important differences.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the physiology of the cochlea, and in particular with the physiology of its sensory cells, the hair cells.
the development of the cochlea and the physiology of the cochlear hair cells.
the development and use of an experimental model of the mammalian cochlea in vitro.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the hair cells of the organotypic mouse cochlea in culture are functionally similar to those of the in vivo guinea pig cochlea, although the OHCs in vitro are less excitable than those in vivo.
the IHCs in the mouse cochleas in organotypic explant culture behave like IHCs in situ in the guinea-pigs and the OHCs behave like OHCs in situ but are not as well developed.
mouse hair cells are similar to guinea-pig hair cells in many respects but differ in some others.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the basic transduction mechanisms are similar in the mouse cochlear hair cells to those in the cochlear hair cells of other mammalian species.
mouse cochlear hair cells exhibit the same basic electrical properties as those of the cochleas from other mammalian species.
the hair cells of the mouse cochlear explant culture retain many morphological and electrophysiological characteristics of the mature cochlea.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the hair cells of the cochlea are capable of generating receptor potentials in response to mechanical stimulation in vitro.
mouse IHCs and mouse OHCs exhibit similar physiological properties to guinea-pig hair cells.
the mouse cochlea can be maintained in vitro for several days without the hair cells losing their ability to respond to mechanical stimulation.
